title: A Robot Dog Outran the Average Human in a Marathon — on One Charge
summary:
Most robots that finish a marathon have wheels. RAIBO2 has legs. That's what makes its 26.2-mile run so impressive.

The quadruped, built by engineers in South Korea, completed the Sangju Dried Persimmon Marathon in 4 hours, 19 minutes, and 52 seconds. The global average marathon time for humans is about 4 hours and 32 minutes. RAIBO2 beat that — and it did it on a single battery charge, finishing with more than a third of its power still left. It averaged 5.9 miles per hour, roughly the pace of a brisk jog for most casual runners. Details about the event and the robot were recently published in the journal Nature.

Why is that hard? Legged robots don't just spend energy moving forward. They also have to constantly support their own body weight and recover energy lost with every step. Before RAIBO2, most quadruped robots could only travel around 12 miles. That's a problem for robot dogs designed for search-and-rescue missions or other jobs that require long distances.

So the team redesigned everything. They made the limbs lighter, built a more efficient motor board, and added a bigger battery with 2,016 watt-hours of capacity. They also changed how RAIBO2 moves — using reinforcement learning in a computer simulation, rewarding the robot every time it placed its feet softly without slipping or overheating. The result is a steady, gentle gait.

The course wasn't easy. The winding route had 938 feet of total elevation change and some slippery spots. RAIBO2 finished without crashing or catching fire — something other running robots have struggled with.

One catch: a human operator steered it using a camera mounted on its head. Building a fully autonomous version would require more computing power, which would drain the battery faster. Still, RAIBO2's energy efficiency — measured at 0.25 cost of transport, compared to 0.37 for an average human runner — marks a real technical advance. The researchers say it's the first robot to outperform humans on that measurement. It deserves a pat on its metal back.
why_it_matters: Energy-efficient legs could send robots into places where a dead battery is dangerous — collapsed buildings, wildfires, long search routes — and the cost-of-transport metric suggests machines are starting to be measured against living bodies rather than against other machines.

background_read: Legged robots are far harder to build than wheeled ones. Boston Dynamics (a U.S. robotics company known for animal-like machines) unveiled BigDog, a four-legged robot built for rough terrain, in 2005, and Honda's ASIMO showed how easily a two-legged robot can fall over — which is why most long-distance robots, such as the Mars rovers, roll on wheels instead.

The journal Nature (a leading international science magazine, first published in 1869) printed the RAIBO2 results, meaning other scientists examined the claims before publication. That review process is part of why the 'first robot to outperform humans' claim carries weight.

'Reinforcement learning' is a training method borrowed from how animals learn: a program tries thousands of actions in a simulation and gets rewarded for the ones that work, gradually discovering a smooth, energy-saving walking style without being told exactly how to move.
The Sangju Dried Persimmon Marathon is a real public race in South Korea, which is why the team could compare RAIBO2 directly with ordinary human runners instead of a robot-only benchmark.

Efficiency here is measured by 'cost of transport' — the energy needed to move a certain distance. Humans are unusually efficient walkers, so beating the human figure is a milestone roboticists have chased for decades.

perspectives.description: They read RAIBO2 as proof that legs do not have to be the expensive option. A cost of transport of 0.25, better than an average human's 0.37, suggests long-distance legged machines are finally practical for search-and-rescue work.

They point out that a human was steering with a camera on the robot's head, that the course was closed and measured, and that the walking style was learned inside a simulation. A controlled marathon is not the same as an autonomous robot working in rubble.

For them the real lesson is a pattern: breakthroughs in robotics come from redesigning hardware and software together. Lighter limbs, a better motor board, a bigger battery and reinforcement learning each mattered, but only as a package.

If the trend continues, legged robots could take over deliveries, inspections and disaster response. The open question is whether the heavy computing needed for full autonomy will always cancel out the battery gains — and who is accountable when such a machine fails on its own.
